Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

tidystata 0.4.1

  • findit(), findit_selection() and findit_clip() share one help topic, including editor and clipboard guidance.

  • capture() and the preparation, summary, correlation and preview helpers have shorter help organized around practical tasks.

  • Both READMEs use the bare-command form findit(reg, robust) and simpler frequency-table headings.

tidystata 0.4.0

  • findit() and the bilingual Stata-to-R reference correct advanced statistical mappings and omit pairs without a close R counterpart. Bayesian examples use explicit posterior summaries and fitted-model prediction methods; IPW examples estimate treatment effects with joint uncertainty.

  • The bilingual Stata-to-R reference opens as smaller subject chapters within the package website, with chapter navigation and expandable alternatives.

  • findit() customizes catalogue examples from Stata text enclosed in backticks or strings, including findit(`tab sex region`, row) and findit("tab sex region, row"). New findit_selection() and findit_clip() look up one command from the source editor or clipboard and print the result. The selection helper is registered as the Find Stata equivalent addin.

  • findit() omits built-in package labels and unnecessary namespace prefixes from printed examples, retaining qualification for conflicting names. Returned code and package metadata are preserved. Moving averages use zoo::rollapply() with partial windows and nonmissing values.

  • destring() and tostring() ignore AsIs wrappers on non-character input. tostring() writes measured values and durations without exponents in their existing units; its help clarifies that large numeric IDs can lose digits.

  • as_character() is now an exact alias of tostring(), converting stored codes to text without reading value labels. Use decode() for the previous label-reading behavior. New encode() creates labelled integer codes from character categories, or preserves factor codes and levels as value labels. Re-encoding decoded text assigns fresh codes and need not restore old codes.

  • destring() accepts non-breaking spaces and drops input names from problems(). destring(), tostring() and decode() now reject data frames instead of returning one value per column.

  • pct() is removed; use pc() for percentages of a total. findit() distinguishes z-scores, total shares and percentile ranks, with executable examples using dplyr::percent_rank() on 0-1 and 0-100 scales.

  • as_dummy() (tab_gen()) supports .names = "label" for value-label names. The default "value" uses original values (raw codes for labelled vectors), while "index" uses consecutive category numbers.

  • corr(), pwcorr() and spearman() share one help page and a dedicated correlation section in the website reference, with guidance on their different defaults and supported options.

  • Head/tail preview omission markers align with printed numeric decimal points, or the last significand digit when no decimal is displayed. Row-number markers align with the last digit; other column types keep centered markers. Unicode output uses vertical ellipses, with periods as the fallback.

  • findit() separates family browsing from specific queries, retains at most ten ambiguous candidates, and prefers matching tidystata helpers before tidyverse and other implementations. Row recipes now use row_mean() and related helpers; footers distinguish relevant results from broader operations. About 90 common data-management lookups that previously offered only base R, such as tabstat, isid, misstable, sort, keep/drop if and egen summaries, now recommend tidystata or tidyverse code and keep base R as an alternative. drop if and replace ... if recipes use dplyr 1.2’s filter_out() and replace_when(), with notes for older dplyr. Negated conditions such as keep if !missing(x) no longer match their opposite.

  • summ() and tabstat() report omitted non-numeric columns and the */**/ *** markers for labelled, factor and retained non-numeric variables as messages rather than warnings; silence them with suppressMessages(). Entirely missing columns and skipped date statistics still warn.

  • summ() and tabstat() reuse native scratch storage for numerical summaries, weighted statistics and grouped distinct counts, reducing temporary allocation. Large two-column categorical tabulations use bounded native counting when a dense integer, logical or factor key is available. Other tabulations retain the general counting path. Public interfaces and statistical rules are unchanged.

  • pwcorr(), corr() and spearman() compute every variable pair natively instead of allocating a row mask and subsets for each pair. Pearson and Spearman results, including p-values, are identical; Spearman tables on 100,000 rows and 30 variables take seconds instead of a minute, and temporary allocation falls from gigabytes to megabytes. Integer, logical and labelled columns are read without conversion; SPSS-labelled columns are still converted so that their user-missing codes are excluded. Native correlation calculations preserve R’s intermediate rounding on Apple Silicon builds.

  • Row functions such as row_max() and row_sum(), and summ()/tabstat(), read integer, logical and numeric labelled columns in place rather than copying them to doubles. Row functions also accept the same vector more than once, as Stata’s egen rowmax(x x) does.

  • var_type() retains full primary class names when abbr = FALSE and the display label is a default class abbreviation, including S4 and S7 classes. Custom display labels and compact output are preserved; codebook() uses the improved descriptive labels.

  • as_dummy() (tab_gen()) expands ordered factors instead of failing with an internal type error.

  • cut_length() reports infinite values and empty input with a clear error; NaN counts as missing. cut_breaks() returns an empty ordered factor for empty input without base-R range warnings.

  • mvdecode(), mvencode(), na_if_value() and value_if_na() report a value whose type does not match x with an error naming mv or value.

  • tostring() writes at most 15 significant digits for very large or small numbers, instead of platform-dependent extra digits. tostring() and the interval labels of xtile(), cut_length() and cut_breaks() use a decimal point whatever options(OutDec) says.

  • summ(), tabstat(), tab2(), fre2(), codebook(), browse(), ds(), variables(), variables_search() and select_or_transmute() reject objects that are not data frames, such as dbplyr lazy tables and arrow tables, with the same .data error as tab(); ds(), variables() and variables_search() previously listed the object’s internal components.

  • New stress tests check every exported function against adversarial column types, shapes and containers, plus invariants for row order, grouping, weights and round trips.

  • New stata_recode() (alias recode()) recodes numeric values with Stata’s recode rules inside mutate(): 1:5 ~ 1 selects the closed range 1 to 5, including decimals; c(1, 3:5) combines values and ranges; min, max and NA select the ends and missing values. The first matching rule wins, unmatched values are kept unless .default replaces them, and named rules label the new codes. The recode() alias and the superseded dplyr::recode() mask each other, depending on attach order; stata_recode() always works. findit("recode") lists the new examples. Matching now uses C++ without per-rule row masks or expanded scalar defaults, reducing allocation on large vectors while retaining ordered rules, numeric types, value labels and SPSS/tagged missing-value handling. Integer input stays integer when every code and .default is a whole number, so 1:5 ~ 1 keeps an integer variable’s storage type, as in Stata.

  • summ() and tabstat() retain defined weighted skewness and kurtosis when fractional frequency weights total at most one, without grouped square-root warnings. Weighted means and shape statistics avoid overflow from large finite weights; reported frequency totals and weighted sums keep their scale.

  • as_dummy() preserves generated indicators that replace removed source names in data.table inputs. It reports an error when removing every column would discard rows from a data.table, with guidance to retain a column.

  • misstable() applies structured-column missingness to list-backed matrices instead of indexing their cell masks as rows.

  • Function help and migration guidance clarify missing-key ordering, duplicate identities, grouped assertions, panel units, binning boundaries and weights, signed standardisation, and Spearman’s small-sample p-values. Bilingual findit() descriptions distinguish variable labels from value labels.

  • pwcorr() and spearman() preserve very small nonzero p-values under Sidak adjustment. Weighted pwcorr() and corr() retain defined correlations when unequal weights make the variance product underflow.

  • Rename the persistent preview helpers to preview() and unpreview(), with preview_headtail() and preview_interval() shortcuts. Remove the former preview names and row-slicing helpers without compatibility aliases. Head/tail output marks an omitted middle with aligned dots; interval output retains its compact layout. Persistent previews and one-time printers have separate help topics.

  • New spearman() computes Spearman rank correlations like Stata’s spearman: one common complete sample by default, .pairwise = TRUE for spearman, pw, and Stata 18’s beta-approximation p-values. The Spearman p-values of pwcorr(.method = "spearman") now use the same method instead of the t approximation of earlier Stata versions, so they change slightly.

  • pwcorr() gains .listwise (Stata’s pwcorr, listwise) and .adjust ("bonferroni" or "sidak", Stata’s options of the same names).

  • ds(), summ(), and tabstat() accept .type = "tibble" to return one tibble regardless of the input’s table class or preview settings. Summary families combine as in table output; existing defaults are unchanged.

  • findit() refreshes bilingual function descriptions and notes for current contracts, with reverse lookup descriptions for every tidystata function.

  • Shared help pages compare related functions and aliases in opening bullets. Grouping, labels, cutting edge cases and examples reflect current behavior.

  • isid() confirms successful key checks with a message while returning the original data invisibly. Use suppressMessages() for silent execution. .missing replaces .missok without an alias; update existing calls. Empty strings, including empty-string factor values, are rejected by default; .missing = TRUE allows them and other missing values but still requires unique key combinations.

  • capture() returns the expression’s result on success and invisible NULL on error, replacing its previous TRUE/FALSE result. It preserves successful visibility and evaluates once. Caught errors emit a failure message by default that chains the original error, keeping its call and bullets; quiet = TRUE suppresses it along with warnings and messages from the expression. Printed output is retained. Put assignments inside capture() to preserve existing objects on failure. Existing Boolean uses must be updated.

  • corr() calculates Pearson correlations on a common complete-case sample, like Stata’s corr (correlate), with tidy selection, computed columns, groups, weights, and long or wide tibble output.

tidystata 0.3.2

  • assert() protects input columns from internal-name collisions and rejects matrix conditions instead of reporting nonexistent row numbers.

  • summ() excludes zero-weight observations from weighted arithmetic, scales large analytic weights safely, and avoids overflow when averaging percentile boundaries. Weighted percentiles retain their values for large finite weights. Datetimes with an empty timezone attribute are accepted. Summary and tabulation help distinguish analytic weights from survey-design inference.

  • summ(), the tabulation family and pwcorr() retain a grouping column when it is also the weight column in an implicit all-column selection.

  • stata_merge() retains shared non-key values on using-only rows while preserving master values, including missing values, on matched rows.

  • cut_length() and cut_breaks() omit SPSS user-missing values before computing intervals. Binning functions reject integer64 inputs with an explicit-conversion message instead of reading their underlying payloads.

  • row_min() and row_max() recognize .data[[column]] inputs in one-row groups and keep .env scalars from filling otherwise all-missing rows.

  • tostring() writes numbers in full, as Stata does: 100000 gives "100000", not "1e+05". destring() reads labelled text like plain text, so ignore, its warning and readr::problems() apply, and rejects a doubled sign such as "-$-5".

  • misstable() counts SPSS user-missing codes and ranges. List columns use the established summary rule: scalar NA elements are missing and NULL elements are observed values. Grouping names that collide with its result columns give a clear error.

  • row_min()/row_max() treat .values columns as columns in one-row groups, and a missing constant makes rows missing when na.rm = FALSE, as in pmin().

  • stata_merge() keeps the master key when using has a non-key column of the same name; cut_breaks() warns when the default median does not split the values and rejects missing breaks and all-missing input.

  • Fixes: tab2() and fre2() no longer tabulate grouping or weight columns without .by, keep factor order around blank headers and compute Cramer’s V for large 2 x 2 tables; summ(.missing = FALSE) accepts weight vectors; as_dummy() handles columns without observed values; is_first() accepts pick(); malformed varlist() ranges, NA positions and var_type(abbr = NA) give clear errors; pc() is missing for an infinite total; the timer no longer prints 60.00s.

tidystata 0.3.1

  • findit() corrects audited statistical mappings, missing-value handling and estimator defaults, with explicit bilingual qualifications and command-specific sources. Name substitution, documented abbreviations, row-number queries, by-prefix options and Chinese chart questions work while example anchors stay stable. Earlier curated examples show their notes in compact output too.

  • Add a searchable English/Chinese Stata-to-R reference book, generated from the findit() catalogue, with chapter navigation and a matching-page language switch. A dedicated pkgdown navigation link opens the book on the author’s website.

  • Expand the bilingual findit() reference with executable, source-linked examples and selected alternative R approaches. The generated guide provides an alphabetical command index, subject tables and a package-sorted R index.

  • Keep concise defaults while showing qualifications and sources on explicit expansion. Stable example IDs allow several R answers for the same Stata code.

  • Respect package-qualified R queries, avoid unrelated word-fragment matches, and explain known gaps and unrepresented option combinations.

  • findit() shows a single clear default, retaining alternatives for ambiguous inputs. Comma-separated variable names and hints customize catalogue examples, as in findit(tab, sex, region) and findit(tab, gen); all matches remain available through print(n = Inf).

tidystata 0.3.0

  • Renamed from statart to tidystata, with a focus on data exploration and preparation. Legacy import/export, regression and plotting wrappers are removed.
  • findit() translates Stata commands, R function names and plain questions into working examples, with English and Chinese guides. In consoles with colour, the Stata and R code retain automatic console colours. Results start with compact example blocks, omit redundant function notes and count remaining examples explicitly.
  • Expanded tabulation and summaries include cross-tables, weights, correlations, missing-value reports and grouped calculations.
  • Added key checks, duplicate handling, Stata-style merges, panel operators, variable transformations and persistent table previews.
  • Statistical conventions follow Stata and are checked against its output. Tables preserve the input container; missing values and labels are handled consistently. See the articles and function reference for details.
  • Faster row calculations and grouped aggregation, with fewer required dependencies. Requires R 4.1.0 and dplyr 1.1.4 or later; flextable is optional.

tidystata 0.2.0

  • Initial CRAN submission.
